extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate and graduate students writing research reports, and their teachers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning, drafting, and revising academic research reports, with sentence-level style rules, revision diagnostics, assignment design features for teachers, and research-ethics standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin sentences with familiar information (first 6–7 words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the first six or seven words refer to familiar information, usually something you have mentioned before (typically your main characters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnose by highlighting the first five or six words in every sentence (ignore short introductory phrases). These beginning words should form a consistent set of related words naming people or concepts readers will recognize; otherwise revise. If they do not include a subject that names a character and a verb that names an important action, revise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Old-before-new principle
rubrics_metrics.description: When clauses conflict between beginning with a character or with old information, always choose the principle of old before new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Older information usually names a character (after you introduce it). Use sentence openings to pick up on familiar referents from prior sentences so passages 'flow' (example contrast: 11a vs 11b where 11b flows because it begins with 'these rain forests' introduced earlier).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use passive/active to serve old-before-new, not dogma
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide active vs passive by whether sentences begin with familiar information (preferably a main character); use passive if it lets you begin with older information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not follow blanket advice to avoid passives. Example: passive moved older info from sentence end to beginning and improved flow (11b). Use passive to describe processes anyone can repeat (e.g., 'Eye movements were measured...'). Use active and first person when referring to actions that only the author/researcher can perform or claim (e.g., 'We conclude...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose active first person for author-specific acts and claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Use active verbs and first-person subjects when authors refer to actions only the writer/researcher can perform (rhetorical actions like suggest, conclude, argue, show; or research acts that merit credit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hiding authorial responsibility when the claim or action is uniquely the author's; the active changes the story appropriately. Example contrast: 'It can be concluded...' vs 'We conclude...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complexity last (put new/complex info at sentence end)
rubrics_metrics.description: If familiar information goes first, the newest, most complex information goes last.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is especially important when introducing a new technical term, presenting a long/complex unit, or introducing a concept to be developed. Structure sentences so technical terms and long complex units appear near the end (example 14a vs 14b and revisiting 11a/11b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce technical terms at the sentence end
rubrics_metrics.description: When you introduce technical terms new to your readers, construct your sentences so those terms appear in the last few words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare versions that front-load jargon versus versions that place technical terms later for readability (example 14a/front-loaded vs 14b/terms last).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not begin sentences with long, complex subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Put complex bundles of ideas that require long phrases or clauses at the end of a sentence, never at the beginning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long subjects at the start make sentences hard to read; flip short familiar information to the beginning (using passive if necessary) and long/complex information to the end for smoother flow (see 11a vs 11b).

rubrics_metrics.name: When starting a paragraph, end early sentences with key terms to be developed
rubrics_metrics.description: Put at the end of the paragraph's first or second sentence the key terms that appear in the rest of the paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare openings to see which better introduce what follows (example 15a vs 15b). If the last few words of the opening are not the most important/complex/weighty, revise so they are.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity & Flow diagnostic: highlight sentence openings
rubrics_metrics.description: To diagnose clarity and flow: highlight the first five or six words in every sentence (ignore brief introductory phrases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run your eye down the page to check whether highlighted openings form a consistent set of related words that name people or concepts readers will recognize. If not, revise. Check that each highlighted opening includes a subject naming a character and a verb naming an important action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision steps for sentence openings
rubrics_metrics.description: To revise openings: identify your main characters, make them the subjects of verbs; convert nominalizations into verbs; ensure each sentence begins with familiar information, preferably a previously mentioned character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for nouns ending in -tion, -ment, -met, etc.; if they are subjects, turn them into verbs. Make characters the grammatical subjects to improve clarity and flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: For emphasis: check sentence endings (underline last 4–5 words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Underline the last four or five words in every sentence; they should include technical-sounding words used for the first time, the newest/most complex information, the most emphatic information, or concepts the next several sentences will develop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you do not see that information in the sentence-ending words, revise to put those words last. Pay special attention to ends of sentences that introduce paragraphs or sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quickest revision strategy: draft first, then revise in steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft without overthinking word-level choices; if you must prioritize revisions, start with passages where you found it hard to explain ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Your first job is to draft something to revise. If short on time, focus on confusing content where sentences tend toward confusion. Then apply the diagnostic and revision steps described above.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spit and polish: check grammar, conventions, and readability
rubrics_metrics.description: After revising style for readability, check grammar, spelling, punctuation, and accepted conventions for numbers, names, foreign words, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While important, detailed rules about sentence length, concision, and word choice are covered in other books; this text focuses on sentence-level readability relevant to research reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical prohibitions for researchers (do nots)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethical researchers do not plagiarize or claim credit for the results of others; do not misreport sources, invent data, or fake results; do not submit data whose accuracy they don't trust unless they say so; do not conceal objections they cannot rebut; do not caricature or distort opposing views; do not destroy data or conceal sources important for those who follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the basic Thou-shall-not list illustrated by historical misconduct examples (fake genetic marks, shredding documents, erasing e-mails, buying papers). Violations weaken the research community and harm the plagiarist's own education and reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical affirmatives: obligations to readers and community
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers should create and honor social contracts with readers: explain why research should change readers' beliefs, examine responsibility to readers if convinced to change, acknowledge readers' alternative views (including strongest objections), and meet other ethical obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research is a collaborative conversation; embracing ethical responsibilities builds trust and benefits both researchers and readers even where agreement on common good is lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designing good research assignments (establish outcomes beyond a product)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good assignments establish outcomes beyond a product to be evaluated: ask students to raise a question or problem they want to resolve and support that resolution with reliable/relevant evidence; translate private interest into a public one by writing for readers who actually need the information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best assignments have students write for real readers (clients, other classes, civic organizations) or simulate such situations so students can imagine readers with real needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designing good assignments (help students learn about their readers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good assignments help students learn about and imagine readers they have never met so they can write plausible reports that meet readers' concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If real readers are inaccessible, teachers can turn the class into its own audience or let students define problems so classmates become plausible readers for one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designing good assignments (create rich contextual scenarios)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good assignments create scenarios rich in contextual information so students can investigate and analyze the situation meaningfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a real context isn't practical, create as much contextual detail as possible and make analysis and discussion of the scenario part of the writing process; social context makes rhetorical choices significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designing good assignments (provide interim readers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good assignments provide interim readers so students solicit early responses from colleagues, friends, family, and the instructor during drafting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build opportunities for peer response into the assignment; train student responders to follow structured diagnostic steps (e.g., chapters 14–17) rather than offering only superficial editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designing good assignments (schedule time and interim deadlines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good assignments give students time and a schedule of interim deadlines to accommodate research's messy, iterative nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide stages for sharing and criticizing progress; allow time for false starts and revision; interim deadlines can reflect the book's outlined sequences and help students monitor progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid imposing empty formal rules; provide meaningful rhetorical context
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasizing formal matters risks trivializing structures into empty drills; teachers must show how formal features answer questions that encourage thinking rather than become mechanical forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers should create rhetorical contexts (real or simulated) that dramatize students' social role as researchers; only teachers can adapt formal steps to students' circumstances and provide necessary social support for beginners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and tolerate messiness in learning research skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginners will produce similar, awkward reports as part of learning; teachers must be patient and provide social support, recognizing that original work often comes later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess students for ability to pose new questions and demonstrate need for solutions; accept that novices may not meet full disciplinary standards immediately and adapt assignments accordingly.
